Below is a little bit about Lipscomb FROM HIS OBITUARY.

1993: Leaves the City Council because of term limits and forms Lipscomb Industries, a chemical supply company.

1994: Lipscomb Industries bids on a city chlorine contract and persuades the council to scrap higher bids. The contract goes to another bidder. The council passes an ethics rule prohibiting former members from doing business with the city for a year after leaving office.

1995: Reclaims his council seat.

1996: Lipscomb Industries is forced into bankruptcy by three creditors claiming more than $100,000 in unpaid debts. The company settles with the creditors but later closes.

1996: Council ally Paul Fielding resigns and pleads guilty to federal charges of extortion and bankruptcy fraud. In court, prosecutors play a 1992 tape in which Mr. Lipscomb and Mr. Fielding purportedly discuss forming a “minority front” company. Mr. Fielding is sent to prison. Mr. Lipscomb is not charged, but speculation begins that he is an FBI target.

1998: Federal authorities inform Mr. Lipscomb that he is under investigation on allegations of bribery, extortion, campaign-finance violations and possible abuse of office.

March 1999: Is indicted with Yellow Cab Co. owner Floyd Richards on 65 counts of bribery and conspiracy. Specifically, Mr. Lipscomb is accused of taking monthly $1,000 cash payments and other gifts from Mr. Richards in exchange for casting votes that helped Yellow Cab. Both plead not guilty.

May 1999: Is re-elected to the council.

December 1999: U.S. District Judge Joe Kendall moves the Lipscomb and Richards trails to Amarillo. Two days later, Mr. Richards cuts a deal with prosecutors and agrees to testify against Mr. Lipscomb.

January 2000: Jurors find Mr. Lipscomb guilty of all 65 counts. “I have sent a real bad odor through the city I love,” he tells U.S. District Judge Joe Kendall upon conviction. However, Mr. Lipscomb never admitted corrupt voting.

February 2000: Resigns from the council. “This is one of the hardest days of my life,” he says.

March 2000: Mr. Lipscomb’s mother, anti-poverty crusader Lucille Jeffrey, dies at age 101.

April 2000: Mr. Lipscomb is sentenced to 41 months of home confinement. He had faced up to 645 years in prison and a $16.2 million fine, prosecutors said.

July 2002: An appellate court sets Mr. Lipscomb free, 27 months into his sentence, after finding that Judge Kendall had abused his discretion by moving the trial to Amarillo over the defense’s objections. “I want to fall on my knees,” a rejoicing Mr. Lipscomb says.

August 2002: U.S. Attorney Jane Boyle announces she will not retry Mr. Lipscomb, in spite of what she called overwhelming evidence of corruption. A second trial would “not serve the interests of justice,” she says.

February 2003: Mr. Lipscomb announces a possible run for mayor “because no one has been proactive in dealing with [Dallas Mayor] Laura Miller.” Days later, he says he won’t run.

August 2003: A day after the abrupt firing of Terrell Bolton, Dallas’ first black police chief, the City Council appoints Mr. Lipscomb to the city’s Citizens Police Review Board.

January 2005: Likens Ms. Miller to Adolf Hitler and compares efforts to expand mayoral powers to Nazi power grabs and the Jewish Holocaust. He apologizes days later.

March 2005: Falls to political protégé James Fantroy in a bid for City Council.

Spring 2010: Suffers a broken right leg in a fall.

June 18, 2011: Dies at age 86.

SOURCES: Dallas Morning News research; Big D: Triumphs and Troubles of an American Supercity in the 20th Century, by Darwin Payne; and Dallas city records
